title: Cash Flow Hedging: How to Protect Margins and Reduce FX Risk
summary: Cash Flow Hedging: How to Protect Margins and Reduce FX Risk

Reduced Uncertainty 2. Improved Financial Planning 3. Optimized Cash Management and Liquidity Planning How Treasury Teams Implement Cash Flow Hedging Programs How Rolling FX Hedge Programs Work Why Layered FX Hedging Is Considered Best Practice How Cash Flow Hedging Improves Firm Value Value Creation Beyond Protection FAQs Cash Flow Hedging: How to Protect Margins and Reduce FX Risk In an earlier article, I outlined how FX exposure flows through a business, from budget to financial statements. This piece builds on that, focusing on how cash flow hedging allows treasury and finance teams to protect margins and reduce FX-driven earnings volatility before it ever reaches the P&L. Currency movements are an uncompensated risk : material and unpredictable. These movements can affect profitability, operating margins, cash flow, and working capital management. Ultimately, they affect the solvency and valuation of all organizations exposed to them. Why FX Risk Is Different from Other Business Risks For businesses operating across currencies , managing FX risk is essential to protecting operating margins and financial stability. Currency exposures , as they relate to how a business operates, have a lifecycle . Currency impacts can be traced from budget to recognition, balance sheet, and then earnings. This lifecycle determines how currency affects forecasts, financial statements, and firm value. FX rate movements can hit expected margins and cash flows long before they are recognized on financial statements. Since foreign exchange moves can drive variances against budget and cash forecasts that are material, cash flow hedging is often employed as the first step in protecting a business from currency risk. Cash flow hedging allows treasury and finance teams to reduce FX-driven earnings volatility and cash flow volatility. Cash Flow Hedging Outcomes: What Businesses Achieve Businesses employ FX hedging against forecasted cash flows to achieve the following : 1. Reduced Uncertainty Until a transaction is recognized, its actual economic value is uncertain. Even developed market currencies can move a few percentage points a month. This sort of 'known unknown' presents uncertainty to margins and cash flows that many businesses can't afford to have. FX hedging helps lock in exchange rates and reduce exposure to unpredictable currency movements. 2. Improved Financial Planning By removing the 'noise' of FX, management can hold departments accountable for actual performance (sales volume, cost control) rather than rewarding or punishing them for market swings. Improved planning can improve competitive position. It allows FP&A teams to evaluate operational performance independently of FX volatility. 3. Optimized Cash Management and Liquidity Planning Volatility in FX rates drives volatility in cash flow. Since cash is the lifeblood of the organization, unhedged cash flows have implications for liquidity, solvency, and valuation. Stable cash flow improves liquidity planning, debt servicing, and working capital management. The following charts use Corpay's Risk Visualizer scenario analysis and hedging strategy development tool to illustrate budget and cash flow at risk under different FX scenarios. Please note that this is a hypothetical example, for illustration only. Corpay Risk Visualizer showing budget and cash flow at risk under different FX scenarios Source: Corpay Treasury Solutions How Treasury Teams Implement Cash Flow Hedging Programs The budget is set. Now what? Effective cash flow hedging programs typically require only an exposure forecast and a budget FX rate. This is fortunate for FP&A teams: the reality is that setting the budget and building the cash forecast is the majority of the work. These forecasts form the foundation for executing an FX hedging strategy . From there, it's a matter of hedge schedule selection, with the two primary choices being a rolling hedge program executed as a strip of hedges or a layered hedge program. The principal differences between these two approaches are in the timing and in the notional amounts of hedges executed per period. However, the results can be very different. Let's assume a business elects to apply a 50% hedge ratio to their forecasted cash flows/budget. The following are hypothetical examples of how the two different hedge schedules operate and the outcomes they drive. How Rolling FX Hedge Programs Work In a rolling program , you typically execute your hedges in large, discrete “blocks” at fixed intervals. Usually these are strips of hedges with differing maturity dates, as shown in the above image. Rolling hedge approaches, though, have their pros and cons . First, you are often 'all-in' on the hedge rate on the day of execution. If the market is at a 12-month low on your execution day, 50% of your entire year's forecast is now locked at that unfavourable rate. More importantly, you are, in essence, simply deferring the impact of FX rate movements on your budget. This effect is especially pronounced if the program is not continuously rolled from one budgeting period into the next, as shown in the USD/PLN Back Test above. This can expose the business to significant FX reset risk when new budget cycles begin. As rates can change materially from one budgeting period to the next, and the business has no ‘protection,’ they will likely be resetting their budgeting process against materially different FX market conditions. That said, many businesses opt for this approach because there is less perceived operational burden . They may also prefer to reset their budgets every year and want a hedge program that is 'set it and forget it.' Why Layered FX Hedging Is Considered Best Practice In a layered hedge program , the same 50% hedge ratio is achieved with hedge rates that vary over the budget and hedge schedule period. This approach is often thought of as best practice , as it avoids the rate cliffs that can occur between periods with rolling and static hedges. The layering also significantly reduces variation in FX rates. Further, as illustrated above, the layered hedge does not simply defer the impact of FX movements. Instead, market volatility is significantly ‘smoothed out’—with well-constructed programs reducing the variation in FX rates by as much as 75% (in my experience). This has a positive knock-on impact on margins, cash flow volatility, and ultimately, firm valuation. The principal downside is that this approach requires more active management, with more frequent execution of hedges. It can also result in hedges that remain on the books of a company across reporting periods and budget cycles, which is not something that every business wants. How Cash Flow Hedging Improves Firm Value Ultimately, finance teams have a choice in how they want to implement a cash flow hedging program, with pros and cons to each choice. That said, cash flow hedging can be more than a delaying tactic or an insurance policy against budget variances. Value Creation Beyond Protection Indeed, effective cash flow hedging can increase firm value via lowering cash flow volatility, improving return on assets by optimizing working capital, and helping managers achieve their budgets more consistently. Reducing FX volatility improves financial predictability, protects margins, and creates the conditions for sustainable, long-term business performance. Additional Resources: Subscribe to our Market Commentary Explore our Currency Research site Book a Meeting with Sean FAQs What is cash flow hedging? Cash flow hedging is the use of financial instruments, such as FX forwards or options, to lock in exchange rates on forecasted foreign currency cash flows. This helps protect margins, stabilize cash flow, and reduce the impact of currency volatility on financial performance. How does cash flow hedging protect margins? Cash flow hedging protects margins by fixing the exchange rate applied to future revenues or expenses. This prevents adverse currency movements from reducing profitability and ensures more predictable financial outcomes. What is the difference between rolling and layered hedge programs? The difference between rolling and layered hedge programs is in the amounts hedged and the duration of the hedge program. Rolling hedges execute large hedge positions at fixed intervals, while layered hedges gradually build hedge coverage, smoothing FX rate exposure and reducing volatility. What is a hedge ratio in FX hedging? A hedge ratio is the percentage of forecasted foreign currency exposure that a company chooses to hedge. For example, a 50% hedge ratio means half of the expected exposure is protected against currency movements. How does cash flow hedging improve financial planning? Cash flow hedging improves financial planning by stabilizing future cash flows and reducing FX-driven budget variances. This allows FP&A teams to evaluate operational performance without distortion from currency volatility. What is FX reset risk? FX reset risk is the exposure a business faces when a new budget cycle begins and existing hedges no longer cover the new period's forecasted cash flows. This typically occurs in rolling hedge programs where hedges expire and are reset under materially different market conditions. What is a hedge schedule? A hedge schedule is the structured plan that defines the timing, notional amounts, and maturity dates of FX hedges executed against a company's forecasted currency exposure. Two common hedge schedules are rolling programs and layered programs. Sean Coakley, CFA Director, Strategic Sales & Market Strategist Sean works with corporate clients and institutional investors focusing on financial risk management, international treasury and working capital optimization. body_text: View All News Eagle Bancorp Montana Earns $3.7 Million, or $0.47 per Diluted Share, in the Second Quarter of 2026, Increases Quarterly Cash Dividend to $0.1475 Per Share July 28, 2026 HELENA, Mont., July 28, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Eagle Bancorp Montana, Inc. (NASDAQ: EBMT), (the “Company,” “Eagle”), the holding company of Opportunity Bank of Montana (the “Bank”), today reported net income of $3.7 million, or $0.47 per diluted share, in the second quarter of 2026, compared to $4.0 million, or $0.51 per diluted share, in the preceding quarter, and $3.2 million, or $0.41 per diluted share, in the second quarter of 2025. In the first six months of 2026, net income increased to $7.7 million, or $0.98 per diluted share, compared to $6.5 million, or $0.83 per diluted share, in the first six months of 2025. Eagle’s board of directors increased its quarterly cash dividend by 1.7% to $0.1475 per share on July 16, 2026. The dividend will be payable on September 4, 2026, to shareholders of record on August 14, 2026. The current dividend represents an annualized yield of 2.63% based on the average closing price of the Company’s common stock reported on NASDAQ during the second quarter of 2026 of $22.44 per share. “Our second quarter results reflect the strength of our franchise and the consistency with which we generate core earnings,” said Laura F. Clark, CEO. “Compared to the same quarter last year, both net income and earnings per share moved higher, a result supported by continued improvement in funding cost alongside resilient asset yields. Net interest margin also continued to expand, climbing to 4.15% for the second quarter. Backed by a strong core deposit base and a well-diversified loan portfolio, we are well positioned to pursue growth opportunities across our footprint and continuing to create lasting value for our shareholders.” Second Quarter 2026 Highlights (at or for the three-month period ended June 30, 2026, except where noted): Net income was $3.7 million, or $0.47 per diluted share, in the second quarter of 2026, compared to $4.0 million, or $0.51 per diluted share in the preceding quarter, and $3.2 million, or $0.41 per diluted share, in the second quarter a year ago. Net interest margin (“NIM”) was 4.15% in the second quarter of 2026, compared to 4.11% in the preceding quarter and 3.91% in the second quarter a year ago. Net interest income, before the provision for credit losses, increased 2.3% to $19.1 million in the second quarter of 2026, compared to $18.7 million in the first quarter of 2026, and increased 5.5% compared to $18.1 million in the second quarter of 2025. Revenues (net interest income before the provision for credit losses, plus noninterest income) were $24.2 million in the second quarter of 2026, compared to $23.6 million in the preceding quarter and $23.0 million in the second quarter a year ago. Total loans of $1.56 billion increased $39.1 million compared to March 31, 2026 and decreased $11.3 million compared to a year earlier. The allowance for credit losses was $17.6 million, or 1.13% of total loans, at June 30, 2026, compared to $17.4 million, or 1.15% of total loans, at March 31, 2026, and $17.7 million, or 1.13% of total loans, a year ago. Total deposits of $1.79 billion remained unchanged compared to March 31, 2026 and increased $52.3 million, or 3.0%, compared to a year earlier. Eagles’s common shareholders’ equity (book value) per share increased to $24.78 at June 30, 2026, compared to $24.22 at March 31, 2026, and $22.72 at June 30, 2025. Tangible book value per share (non-GAAP) increased to $20.07 at June 30, 2026, compared to $19.48 at March 31, 2026, and $17.86 at June 30, 2025. The Company’s available borrowing capacity was approximately $575.0 million at June 30, 2026, compared to $593.1 million at March 31, 2026, and $463.0 million at June 30, 2025. The Company paid a quarterly cash dividend in the second quarter of $0.1450 per share on June 5, 2026, to shareholders of record May 15, 2026. Balance Sheet Results Total assets were $2.13 billion at June 30, 2026, compared to $2.14 billion one year ago, and $2.09 billion three months earlier. The investment securities portfolio totaled $285.7 million at June 30, 2026, compared to $285.0 million a year ago, and $274.9 million at March 31, 2026. Eagle originated $88.1 million in new residential mortgages during the quarter and sold $72.5 million in residential mortgages, with an average gross margin on sale of mortgage loans of approximately 3.07%. This production compares to residential mortgage originations of $75.0 million in the preceding quarter with sales of $66.1 million and an average gross margin on sale of mortgage loans of approximately 2.54%. Total loans decreased $11.3 million compared to a year ago and increased $39.1 million compared to three months earlier. Commercial real estate loans increased to $684.4 million at June 30, 2026, compared to $675.3 million a year earlier. Commercial real estate loans were comprised of 72.1% non-owner occupied and 27.9% owner occupied at June 30, 2026. Agricultural and farmland loans decreased 7.3% to $294.2 million at June 30, 2026, compared to $317.3 million a year earlier. Residential mortgage loans decreased 2.3% to $143.7 million, compared to $147.1 million a year earlier. Commercial loans increased 6.0% to $161.5 million, compared to $152.3 million a year ago. Commercial construction and development loans decreased 2.1% to $98.9 million, compared to $101.0 million a year ago. Home equity loans increased 5.7% to $108.6 million, residential construction loans decreased 3.2% to $45.6 million, and consumer loans decreased 19.5% to $21.5 million, compared to a year ago. “Deposit costs continued a downward trajectory during the second quarter, reflecting the strength of our core deposit base and the favorable repricing of maturing CDs, and we anticipate deposit costs will remain well-managed throughout the remainder of the year, even as the interest rate environment evolves,” said Miranda Spaulding, Chief Financial Officer. Total deposits increased to $1.79 billion at June 30, 2026 from $1.74 billion at June 30, 2025, and remained unchanged compared to March 31, 2026. Noninterest-bearing checking accounts represented 25.0%, interest-bearing checking accounts represented 11.9%, savings accounts represented 11.8%, money market accounts comprised 25.2% and time certificates of deposit made up 26.1% of the total deposit portfolio at June 30, 2026. The average cost of total deposits was 1.49% in the second quarter of 2026, compared to 1.52% in the preceding quarter and 1.62% in the second quarter of 2025. The estimated amount of uninsured deposits was approximately $359.8 million, or 20% of total deposits, at June 30, 2026, compared to $354.1 million, or 20% of total deposits, at March 31, 2026. FHLB advances and other borrowings decreased to $52.1 million at June 30, 2026, compared to $119.4 million at June 30, 2025, and increased compared to $26.7 million at March 31, 2026. The average cost of FHLB advances and other borrowings was 5.30% in the second quarter of 2026, compared to 5.46% in the preceding quarter and 4.65% in the second quarter of 2025. Other borrowings at June 30, 2026 include the Company’s line of credit draw for $13.0 million at an average rate of 6.34% for the second quarter of 2026, compared to $15.0 million at an average rate of 6.34% for the first quarter of 2026. Shareholders’ equity was $197.4 million at June 30, 2026, compared to $180.6 million a year earlier and $193.0 million three months earlier. Book value per share of $24.78 at June 30, 2026, increased 9.1%, compared to $22.72 a year earlier, and increased 2.3%, compared to $24.22 three months earlier. Tangible book value per share, a non-GAAP financial measure calculated by dividing shareholders’ equity, less goodwill and core deposit intangible, by common shares outstanding, of $20.07 at June 30, 2026, increased 12.4%, compared to $17.86 a year earlier and increased 3.0%, compared to $19.48 three months earlier. Operating Results “Our net interest margin improved four-basis points sequentially and expanded 24-basis points over the same period last year, as a meaningful decline in funding costs more than offset modest compression in earning asset yields. With the policy backdrop now pointing toward the potential for rate increases, we are closely monitoring the impact on our liability costs and remain focused on balance sheet positioning to help sustain net interest margin,” said Spaulding. Eagle’s NIM was 4.15% in the second quarter of 2026, compared to 4.11% in the preceding quarter and 3.91% in the second quarter a year ago. The interest accretion on acquired loans totaled $94,000 and resulted in a two-basis point increase in the NIM during the second quarter of 2026, compared to $185,000 and a four-basis point increase in the NIM during the preceding quarter. Average yields on interest earning assets for the second quarter of 2026 were 5.77%, compared to 5.76% in the first quarter of 2026 and 5.85% in the second quarter a year ago. Funding costs for the second quarter of 2026 decreased to 2.12%, compared to 2.15% in the first quarter of 2026 and 2.45% in the second quarter of 2025. For the first six months of 2026, NIM expanded 31 basis points to 4.13% compared to 3.82% for the first six months of 2025. Net interest income, before the provision for credit losses, was $19.1 million in the second quarter of 2026, compared to $18.7 million in the first quarter of 2026, and increased 5.5% compared to $18.1 million in the second quarter of 2025. Year-to-date, net interest income increased 8.0% to $37.8 million, compared to $35.0 million in the same period one year earlier. Revenues for the second quarter of 2026 were $24.2 million, compared to $23.6 million in the preceding quarter and increased 5.2% compared to $23.0 million in the second quarter a year ago. In the first six months of 2026, revenues were $47.7 million, an 8.8% increase compared to $43.9 million in the first six months of 2025. Total noninterest income was $5.0 million in the second quarter of 2026, compared to $4.9 million in the preceding quarter, and increased 4.4% compared to $4.8 million in the second quarter a year ago. In the first six months of 2026, noninterest income increased 12.2% to $9.9 million, compared to $8.8 million in the first six months of 2025. Net mortgage banking income, the largest component of noninterest income, totaled $2.9 million in the second quarter of 2026, compared to $2.4 million in the preceding quarter and $2.9 million in the second quarter a year ago. Net mortgage banking income increased 6.0% to $5.4 million in the first six months of 2026, compared to $5.1 million in the first six months of 2025. “We continue to apply careful financial discipline, all while prioritizing investment in the areas we are confident will drive the greatest long-term impact,” said Darryl Rensmon, President and Chief Operating Officer. Eagle’s second quarter noninterest expense was $19.0 million, compared to $18.2 million in the preceding quarter, and increased 5.9% compared to $17.9 million in the second quarter of 2025. In the first six months of 2026, noninterest expense increased 6.5% to $37.2 million, compared to $34.9 million in the first six months of 2025. The increases to the quarterly and year-to-date non-interest expense relate primarily to increases in salaries and employee benefits. For the second quarter of 2026, the Company recorded income tax expense of $1.1 million, compared to $1.1 million in the preceding quarter and $751,000 in the second quarter of 2025. The effective tax rate for the second quarter of 2026 was 22.9%, compared to 21.8% for the first quarter of 2026 and 18.8% for the second quarter of 2025. The year-to-date effective tax rate was 22.3% for 2026 compared to 17.6% for the same period in 2025. The effective tax rate has increased as the Company’s pretax earnings have increased at a faster pace than tax exempt income. Credit Quality Eagle recorded a $343,000 provision for credit losses for the second quarter of 2026, compared to a $279,000 provision for credit losses in the preceding quarter and a $1.0 million provision for credit losses in the second quarter a year ago. The allowance for credit losses represented 423.5% of nonperforming loans at June 30, 2026, compared to 315.0% three months earlier and 348.8% a year earlier. Nonperforming loans were $4.2 million at June 30, 2026, $5.5 million at March 31, 2026, and $5.1 million a year earlier. Net loan charge-offs totaled $193,000 in the second quarter of 2026, compared to $49,000 in the preceding quarter and $48,000 in the second quarter a year ago. The allowance for credit losses was $17.6 million, or 1.13% of total loans, at June 30, 2026, compared to $17.4 million, or 1.15% of total loans, at March 31, 2026, and $17.7 million, or 1.13% of total loans a year ago. Capital Management Eagles’s ratio of tangible common shareholders’ equity (shareholders’ equity, less goodwill and core deposit intangible) to tangible assets (total assets, less goodwill and core deposit intangible) was 7.66% at June 30, 2026, up from 6.77% a year ago and 7.55% three months earlier. This ratio is a non-GAAP financial measure. For the most comparable GAAP financial measure, see “Reconciliation of Non-GAAP Financial Measures” below. The Bank’s Tier 1 capital to adjusted total average assets was 10.93% as of June 30, 2026. As of June 30, 2026, the Bank’s regulatory capital was in excess of all applicable regulatory requirements and is deemed well capitalized. About the Company Eagle Bancorp Montana, Inc. is a bank holding company headquartered in Helena, Montana, and is the holding company of Opportunity Bank of Montana, a community bank established in 1922 that serves consumers and small businesses in Montana through 30 banking offices. Additional information is available on the Bank’s website at www.opportunitybank.com . Use of Non-GAAP Financial Measures In addition to results presented in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles utilized in the United States, or GAAP, this release, including the Additional Financial Information contains non-GAAP financial measures. Non-GAAP financial measures in this release include: 1) core efficiency ratio, 2) tangible book value per share and 3) tangible common shareholders’ equity to tangible assets. The Company uses these non-GAAP financial measures to provide meaningful supplemental information regarding the Company’s operational performance, performance trends and financial condition, and to enhance investors’ overall understanding of such financial performance. In particular, the use of tangible book value per share and tangible common equity to tangible assets is prevalent among banking regulators, investors and analysts. The numerator for the core efficiency ratio is calculated by subtracting intangible asset amortization from noninterest expense. Tangible assets and tangible common shareholders’ equity are calculated by excluding intangible assets from assets and shareholders’ equity, respectively. For these financial measures, our intangible assets consist of goodwill and core deposit intangible. Tangible book value per share is calculated by dividing tangible common shareholders’ equity by the number of common shares outstanding. We believe that this measure is consistent with the capital treatment by our bank regulatory agencies, which exclude intangible assets from the calculation of risk-based capital ratios and present this measure to facilitate the comparison of the quality and composition of our capital over time and in comparison, to our competitors. Non-GAAP financial measures have inherent limitations, are not required to be uniformly applied, and are not audited. Because non-GAAP financial measures are not standardized, it may not be possible to compare these financial measures with other companies’ non-GAAP financial measures having the same or similar names. Further, the non-GAAP financial measure of tangible book value per share should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for book value per share or total shareholders’ equity determined in accordance with GAAP, and may not be comparable to a similarly titled measure reported by other companies. title: Every Chair is a Revenue Opportunity: Maximizing Revenue and Reducing Risk with Agilysys OnDemand Full Service
summary: Pool decks, beaches, cabanas, and outdoor venues often create unique operational challenges. Guests are often ready to order long before a server is available for their next visit. Every minute spent waiting is a potential missed revenue opportunity.With Agilysys OnDemand Full Service, guests can place additional orders the moment they are ready—whether that’s another cocktail, appetizer, […]
body_text: BLOGS July 22, 2026 David Bain Sales Engineer Connect with David in Linkedin Pool decks, beaches, cabanas, and outdoor venues often create unique operational challenges. Guests are often ready to order long before a server is available for their next visit. Every minute spent waiting is a potential missed revenue opportunity. With Agilysys OnDemand Full Service , guests can place additional orders the moment they are ready—whether that’s another cocktail, appetizer, dessert, or round of drinks—without waiting for a server to return. Orders flow directly into the InfoGenesis POS ecosystem, helping properties capture incremental revenue that might otherwise be missed during busy service periods. Agilysys OnDemand Full Service helps minimize these risks through flexible pre-authorization capabilities that can be initiated by either the guest or a service team member. Guests can securely authorize a payment method before ordering, creating a frictionless experience that allows them to continue ordering throughout their stay without repeatedly presenting a credit card. Alternatively, staff can establish a pre-authorized tab as part of the service experience, allowing operators to maintain traditional high-touch hospitality while protecting revenue. Menus, pricing, and service workflows remain centrally managed through InfoGenesis, helping operators maintain control while expanding service reach. Support Staff Without Increasing Labor Costs Many resorts, casinos, hotels, and clubs struggle to provide adequate service coverage across large pool decks, beaches, and outdoor venues. OnDemand Full Service allows a smaller team to effectively serve more guests. Rather than spending valuable time walking chair-to-chair taking orders, staff can focus on: Delivering food and beverages Building guest relationships Managing service quality Upselling premium offerings This improves labor efficiency while maintaining high service standards during peak periods. Increase Guest Satisfaction and Loyalty Guests today value convenience as much as quality. When someone relaxing in a cabana can order lunch with a few taps—or a guest by the pool can request another beverage without leaving their chair—it creates a frictionless experience that feels modern and personalized. The easier it is for guests to order, the more likely they are to purchase, return, and recommend your property to others. The Bottom Line: By combining self-service ordering with flexible pre-authorization, , properties can confidently expand food and beverage service beyond traditional restaurant settings— maximizing guest spending opportunities while maintaining the high-touch service experience guests expect. Whether serving guests poolside, in private cabanas, on the beach, or throughout the resort, OnDemand Full Service helps operators: ✅ Capture more revenue opportunities ✅ Improve order accuracy ✅ Enhance labor efficiency ✅ Reduce operational risk ✅ Deliver exceptional guest experiences everywhere Because the best seat in the house should always be a place where guests can order—and spend—with ease. Written By David Bain With 10+ years of experience, David specializes in bridging the gap between complex technical integrations and operational success to drive record-breaking business growth.

title: Is Hippo Insurance Legit? An Honest Breakdown
body_text: Hippo Insurance is legitimate: it sells regulated homeowners insurance in the United States and must be licensed in every state where it offers policies. But your actual experience can vary by state and by the underwriting carrier listed on your declarations page,, check the carrier’s financial strength rating, and compare coverage details before you buy. This guide shows you exactly how to do that, then walks through Hippo’s coverage, pricing, claims, and real-world reviews in plain English. Quick verdict Legit? Yes. Hippo is licensed and regulated wherever it sells policies, and you can verify this yourself by state. Like most insurers, satisfaction depends on the specific claim, the underwriting carrier, and local service, so it helps to check complaint patterns and recent claims feedback. Best for: tech-friendly shoppers who will read the policy form and endorsements carefully and who value an online-first, proactive-protection model. Not ideal for: complex or high-risk properties, or anyone who strongly prefers a single local agent for in-person support. Is Hippo Insurance legit? Yes. In insurance terms, a company is legitimate when it is licensed by the state insurance department in each market where it sells coverage, when an admitted underwriting carrier stands behind the policy, and when that carrier carries a financial strength rating that signals it can pay claims. Hippo meets these structural tests. The more useful question is not whether the company is real, but whether a Hippo policy is a strong fit for your home, your state, and your risk profile. That answer depends on details you can check in minutes. Three fast checks tell you almost everything. First, confirm the license: look up the company on your state Department of Insurance (DOI) website to confirm it is authorized to sell homeowners coverage where you live. Second, identify the underwriting carrier:Hippo is a licensed insurance agency that places policies with carrier partners, so the name that actually backs your policy is the one listed on your declarations page, not Hippo. Third, check the financial strength rating of that underwriting carrier through a rating agency such as AM Best, Demotech, KBRA, or Kroll, and note the rating date. If all three check out, you are dealing with a legitimate, regulated product. How to verify any home insurer in four steps. © Hippo Insurance. What is Hippo Insurance, and how does it work? Hippo is a technology-forward home insurance agency built around an online-first experience and a proactive approach to preventing damage before it happens. Rather than positioning itself purely as a claims-payer, Hippo emphasizes fast digital quoting. Functionally, Hippo acts as a managing general agent (MGA): it designs and services the policy and runs the customer experience, while licensed partner carriers underwrite and bear the insurance risk. That structure is common in modern insurance and is one reason the underwriting carrier on your declarations page matters so much. Availability varies by state, and insurers periodically pause new business or adjust where they write coverage based on catastrophe exposure and underwriting guidelines. Is Hippo licensed and regulated? Home insurance is regulated at the state level. Every state has a Department of Insurance that licenses insurers and agencies, reviews policy forms and rates, and handles consumer complaints. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) also publishes consumer tools and a complaint index that lets you compare how often a company generates complaints relative to its size. Because regulation is state-by-state, a company can be fully licensed in one state and not active in another, which is why your own state lookup is the authoritative source. Here is a simple step-by-step way to verify Hippo, or the carrier behind it, in your state. Step one: visit your state DOI website and use its company or license lookup. Step two: search for the insurer and confirm it is authorized for homeowners or property lines. Step three: identify the underwriting carrier named on your quote or declarations page, since the MGA and the carrier can have different names. Step four: look up that carrier’s financial strength rating and its date. Step five: review the NAIC complaint index for the carrier to see whether complaints run above or below the median for its size. If the name on your declarations page does not match the brand you expected, that is normal under the MGA model, not a red flag. Hippo places policies with partner carriers, so the legal entity that pays your claim may be a carrier you have not heard of. The point is simply to confirm that the named carrier is licensed in your state and carries an acceptable financial strength rating. If you cannot find the carrier listed with your DOI, pause and ask Hippo to identify the underwriting entity before you bind coverage. Financial strength: can Hippo pay claims? A financial strength rating is an independent opinion about an insurer’s ability to meet its policyholder obligations, especially after a large or widespread loss event. Agencies such as AM Best, Demotech, KBRA, and Kroll assign these ratings using their own scales and methodologies. Because Hippo policies are underwritten by partner carriers, the rating that matters for your specific policy is the rating of the carrier named on your declarations page, not a single brand-wide grade. To find it, take the carrier name from your quote and search the rating agency’s website for that entity, then note the rating and the date it was issued or affirmed. Ratings can change, so a current rating is more meaningful than one from several years ago. If a carrier is listed as unrated, that does not automatically mean it is weak, but it does mean you should weigh other signals more heavily, such as the carrier’s reinsurance, its complaint history, and how long it has operated in your state. When two policies look similar on price and coverage, the carrier with the stronger, more current rating is generally the safer choice. Coverage: what Hippo homeowners insurance typically includes A Hippo homeowners policy is built on the same standard structure as most policies in the market. Dwelling coverage protects the home itself, other structures coverage applies to detached features like fences and sheds, and personal property coverage helps replace your belongings. Loss of use coverage helps with additional living expenses if a covered loss makes your home uninhabitable, personal liability protection responds if you are found responsible for injury or property damage to others, and medical payments coverage handles smaller medical costs for guests regardless of fault. These are the building blocks you should expect from any reputable homeowners policy. The meaningful differences show up in endorsements and limits. Common optional endorsements worth asking about include water backup coverage for sump pump and sewer backups, service line coverage for buried utility lines, and equipment breakdown coverage for home systems and appliances. Scheduled personal property can raise limits on high-value items like jewelry, and some policies offer identity theft or cyber add-ons. Just as important are the exclusions: standard homeowners policies generally do not cover flood or earthquake, and they exclude wear and tear, neglect, and gradual problems like long-term mold. Read your policy form to confirm which perils are covered, what is capped, and where you may want to add protection. Pricing: is Hippo cheaper? There is no single answer, because home insurance pricing is highly individual. Your premium reflects your location and catastrophe exposure, the age and construction of your home, your coverage limits and deductible, your claims history, and the underwriting carrier’s rates in your state. That means Hippo can be very competitive for one home and middle-of-the-pack for another, even on the same street. The honest framing is that Hippo may be cheaper for some homeowners and not others, and the only way to know is an apples-to-apples comparison. Hippo’s model leans on discounts and smart-home perks, so ask which discounts apply to you, including bundling, new-home or new-roof credits, protective devices, and smart-home monitoring participation. Keep in mind that rates can rise at renewal across the industry when local catastrophe losses, rebuilding costs, or reinsurance prices increase, and a renewal increase is not by itself a sign that a company is acting unfairly. To compare fairly, hold coverage constant: match the dwelling limit, the deductible, the loss settlement basis (replacement cost versus actual cash value), and the same endorsements across every quote. A policy that looks cheaper only because it excludes water backup or settles the roof on an actual cash value basis is not actually cheaper once you account for the gap. Claims: does Hippo pay claims? Yes, covered claims are paid by the underwriting carrier behind your policy, subject to your coverage terms, limits, and deductible. To file, you typically start through Hippo’s app, website, or phone line, and you will move faster if you have your policy number, the date and cause of loss, a clear description of the damage, and photos or video. Documenting the loss early and keeping receipts for emergency repairs and temporary living expenses helps the process go smoothly. A typical claim moves through acknowledgment, inspection or adjuster review, an estimate, and then payment, and simple claims often resolve relatively quickly. Delays usually trace back to a handful of causes: widespread catastrophes that flood adjusters with claims at once, missing documentation, disputes over the cause or scope of damage, or limited contractor and vendor availability in your area. If a claim is delayed or denied, ask for the specific reason in writing and the policy language behind it, supply any additional documentation requested, and request a re-inspection if you disagree with the scope. If you still cannot resolve it, you can escalate to a supervisor, request the carrier’s appraisal process where available, and file a complaint with your state DOI, which insurers are required to respond to. Reviews and complaints: what customers report Online reviews are useful but limited. People are more likely to post after an unusually good or bad experience, review platforms vary in how they verify posts, and a single dramatic story can color your impression more than it should. Read reviews for themes rather than verdicts. On the positive side, Hippo customers often highlight a fast, low-friction online quote and purchase, helpful smart-home perks, and responsive digital service. On the negative side, the most common frustrations across home insurers, Hippo included, tend to involve claim timelines after major events, disputes over roof or water damage scope, and premium increases at renewal. A better signal than star ratings is complaint data. The NAIC complaint index compares how many complaints a company receives relative to its size, where a score of 1.0 is the median. Checking the index for the underwriting carrier on your policy gives you a more objective read than scrolling testimonials, because it is normalized and reported to regulators. Use reviews to understand the experience, and use complaint and rating data to judge reliability. Pros and cons of Hippo Insurance Pros: a fast, online-first quote and purchase experience; a proactive model with smart-home monitoring and home-health perks designed to prevent losses; useful endorsements such as water backup, service line, and equipment breakdown; and discounts that can reward newer homes and connected devices. For homeowners who like managing things digitally and are willing to read the policy form, this combination is appealing. Cons: availability and underwriting carriers vary by state, so the experience is not identical everywhere; the MGA model means the carrier paying your claim may be a name you have to look up; pricing is not universally the lowest and can rise at renewal like the rest of the market; and homeowners who want a single dedicated local agent for in-person help may prefer a traditional insurer. None of these are disqualifying, but they are reasons to verify the details before you buy. Who Hippo is best for, and who should consider alternatives Hippo tends to fit tech-forward homeowners who want a quick online experience, are interested in smart-home discounts and proactive monitoring, and are comfortable comparing policy forms on their own. It also suits first-time buyers who want clear digital tools, as long as they take time to understand deductibles, endorsements, and replacement cost. Homeowners switching after a rate hike can find value here too, provided the coverage matches and the carrier’s rating and complaint data check out. Alternatives are worth a look in a few situations. If you have a complex or high-risk property, or you live in an area with limited availability, a traditional insurer such as State Farm or Allstate, or a specialty market, may offer broader options. If you want everything in one app at the lowest possible entry price and have a simpler home, an insurtech competitor like Lemonade may appeal. The right way to choose is simple: get three to five quotes with identical coverage limits, deductibles, and endorsements; confirm each carrier is licensed in your state and check its financial strength rating and complaint index; and then weigh price against coverage quality and service reputation rather than price alone. Frequently asked questions Is Hippo Insurance a scam? No. Hippo is a legitimate, regulated home insurance company that must be licensed in every state where it sells policies, and its policies are backed by licensed underwriting carriers. You can confirm this through your state Department of Insurance. Is Hippo good at paying claims? Covered claims are paid by the underwriting carrier, subject to your policy terms. Satisfaction varies by claim type and market, so checking the carrier’s NAIC complaint index alongside recent reviews gives you the most realistic picture. Who underwrites Hippo Insurance? Hippo operates as a managing general agent and places policies with partner carriers, so the underwriting carrier is the name listed on your declarations page. That carrier, not the Hippo brand alone, is the entity whose rating and license you should verify. Does Hippo cover water damage? Sudden and accidental water damage is typically covered, but standard policies exclude flood, and sewer or sump pump backups usually require a water backup endorsement. Read your policy form and add endorsements where you need them. Can Hippo cancel or non-renew my policy? Like all insurers, Hippo and its carriers can non-renew or cancel within the rules your state allows, often tied to risk changes, underwriting guidelines, or non-payment. You are entitled to notice and a stated reason, which your state DOI can help you understand. Can I cancel Hippo Insurance anytime? Generally yes. Homeowners can usually cancel and may receive a prorated refund of unearned premium, though if you have a mortgage you will need to line up replacement coverage so there is no lapse your lender would flag. The bottom line Hippo is a legitimate, regulated home insurance company, and for the right homeowner it offers a genuinely modern experience with proactive protection and useful endorsements. The smart move is not to take any brand’s word for it, including this guide, but to verify the specifics for your own home: confirm the license in your state, identify and rate the underwriting carrier on your declarations page, read the coverage and exclusions, and compare quotes on an apples-to-apples basis. Do that, and you can decide with confidence whether Hippo is the right fit or whether another insurer serves your situation better. Next step: compare quotes from three to five insurers with matching coverage limits, then verify each carrier’s license and financial strength rating before you buy. Start your comparison at hippo.com . This article is for general information only and is not financial or insurance advice. Coverage, availability, carrier options, discounts, and ratings vary by state and underwriting guidelines and can change, so read your declarations page and policy forms and verify details before purchasing.
